passage:
Note from Chandrika, class teacher.
At the games period, Ira and another child argued over whether a marble touched the line. "It did!" "It didn't!" Each said it louder, each repeated the same words, and the circle of onlookers grew. Ira's fists were clenched, and neither was listening. I stepped in and said, "Ira, before you answer, tell me what the other person just said." Ira stared, then said, "That it didn't touch. Because it stopped early." I asked the other child the same. They were quiet for a moment. Then Ira said, "Okay. Let's look at the line together." I will try this again next week.

qa.q: What did the children argue about?
qa.a: Whether a marble touched the line.

qa.q: What was Ira wanting during the argument, judging by the clenched fists and the loud repeats?
qa.a: Angry and set on winning, with clenched fists and loud repeats, rather than trying to understand the other child.

qa.q: What did Chandrika suggest that started to change the pattern?
qa.a: Chandrika asked Ira to say what the other person had just said before answering.

qa.q: How might the other child have felt when Ira repeated the point about the marble stopping early?
qa.a: Heard and a bit surprised, since the other point was said aloud and the shouting stopped, making it easier to look at the line together.

grounding: Children arguing over a game push louder and repeat the same claim; stating what the other said before answering begins to change the pattern.

passage:
Sunday night. Today Salma and I had a big fight in the carrom game. I said the coin was in the pocket, Salma said it wasn't, and we both got louder and louder, until Mummy came and said, "Karthik, tell Salma what she said, before you say your thing." I was so cross. But I tried. "You said the coin didn't go in because it touched the edge." Salma's face changed. "Yes! You heard me." Then she said, "You said it went in because the edge is soft?" "Yes." It was so strange. We looked at the board together, and there was a little dent. We both laughed.
Karthik

qa.q: What game did Karthik and Salma play?
qa.a: Carrom.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling when Mummy said to repeat what Salma said?
qa.a: Cross, though Karthik tried anyway. Wanting to win made it hard to listen at first.

qa.q: What did Karthik do that changed the fight?
qa.a: Karthik said back what Salma had said before giving Karthik's own view, and then they looked at the board together.

qa.q: How might Salma have felt when Karthik repeated what she said?
qa.a: Heard and happier, since her face changed and she said "You heard me," then repeated Karthik's view in turn.

grounding: Children arguing over a game push louder; stating what the other person said before answering changes the pattern.

passage:
Last Sunday, Aparna and I were playing snakes and ladders at her house, and we had the biggest fight. She said if you land on a ladder with a six, you get another turn. I said no, you don't. "Yes, you do!" "No, you DON'T!" We got louder and louder, saying the same thing again and again. Her mother came in.
She said, "Swati, before you answer, tell me what Aparna said." I was annoyed. "She said you get another turn." "Aparna, what did Swati say?" "That you don't." Then Aunty asked, "Why do you each think so?"
Aparna said her Nani plays that way. I said my book says no. Then we just decided to play Nani's way at Aparna's house, and the book way at mine.
I'm still not sure who's right. But we stopped shouting.

qa.q: What game were Swati and Aparna playing?
qa.a: Snakes and ladders.

qa.q: What was Swati feeling when asked to repeat what Aparna said?
qa.a: Swati felt annoyed at first, wanting to win the argument.

qa.q: What small step changed the argument?
qa.a: Saying back what the other person said before answering, and asking why each thought so, which helped them understand each other.

qa.q: How might Aparna have felt when Swati repeated her point?
qa.a: Aparna probably felt heard, which made it easier to explain her Nani's rule calmly.

grounding: Shows children arguing over a game by repeating their claims louder, and stating the other's view first starting to change the pattern.

passage:
Class 5 teacher's note, Wednesday.
At break, Vidya and Pranav were shouting over a cricket game. "You were OUT!" "I was NOT out!" Twelve times at least, each louder. Neither was listening.
I stepped in and made a rule: before you answer, you have to say what the other person just said. Pranav rolled his eyes. "She thinks I was out because the ball hit the stumps." Vidya said, "He thinks he wasn't out because the bail didn't fall." They both paused. Then Pranav said, "Oh. That's actually the real question."
They asked the PE teacher, who said the bail must fall. Vidya accepted it. I'll teach the "say it back" rule to the whole class on Friday.

qa.q: What did the PE teacher say about the bail?
qa.a: The bail must fall for a batter to be out.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling when he realised the real question?
qa.a: He seemed surprised and more open, no longer just angry, once he heard Vidya's point clearly.

qa.q: What did the teacher's rule change, and why?
qa.a: Saying back what the other said forced them to listen, which showed them the real disagreement about the bail.

qa.q: How did Vidya respond to the PE teacher's answer?
qa.a: She accepted it, which suggests she felt the argument had been fair.

grounding: Shows children arguing louder over a game until stating what the other said helps them understand each other.

passage:
Tuesday
Sangeeta and I had a huge fight over hopscotch today. She said I stepped on the line. I said I didn't. We kept shouting "You did!" "I didn't!" until Didi came out and said we sounded like two crows.
Then Didi told us a trick: before you answer, say back what the other one said. I didn't want to. But I said, "Sangeeta says my foot touched the line." She said, "Trisha says her foot was inside." Then I said, "Maybe my toe touched it. Just a little."
Sangeeta laughed. "Okay, maybe just a little." We decided to redo my turn.
It was so weird. When I said her words, I stopped wanting to win so much.
Trisha

qa.q: What did Didi say they sounded like?
qa.a: Two crows.

qa.q: How did Trisha feel after saying Sangeeta's words?
qa.a: Trisha felt less stubborn, no longer wanting to win so much.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Saying back what the other person said worked, because it made both girls listen and admit a little.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta respond when Trisha admitted her toe touched?
qa.a: She laughed and admitted 'maybe just a little', agreeing to redo the turn.

grounding: Shows children arguing louder over a game until repeating the other's view helps them understand and settle it.

passage: Behind the chapel in the village, Maria and Farida crouched over hopscotch squares scratched in the red dirt. "Your foot touched the line! Out!" Maria shouted. "It did not!" "It did!" "Did NOT!" Each time Maria said it louder, Farida said it louder back, until a goat trotted away. Jude, mending a fishing net nearby, called, "Maria, before you answer, say what Farida just said." Maria scowled. "She says... her heel was on the line but her toes were inside." She stopped. That was different from what she had been fighting about. "So only your heel?" Farida nodded, still frowning. They had never decided what counts. Heels count, they agreed, and Farida hopped again, carefully.

qa.q: Where were the hopscotch squares?
qa.a: They were scratched in the red dirt behind the chapel in the village.

qa.q: Why did Maria scowl when Jude spoke up?
qa.a: Maria felt annoyed at being stopped mid-argument and still wanted to win, so saying Farida's side out loud felt like giving in.

qa.q: What could the two try the next time a game argument starts?
qa.a: Each could say back the other's point first, like "you mean only your heel?", and then agree on a rule together.

qa.q: How might Farida have felt once Maria repeated her point?
qa.a: Farida likely felt heard for the first time in the quarrel, which let her calm down enough to agree on a rule, though she was still a bit cross.

grounding: Shows children shouting the same claim louder over a game until one of them says back what the other said, which starts to change the pattern.
